subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-151 now before the House seeks to provide the Government with authority to borrow $14.7 billion. That money is needed because, as has been the case from the time the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office 15 years ago, the Government's uncontrolled expenditures have greatly exceeded its revenues. Indeed, this is the seventh time in the current session that the Government has had to come to Parliament, cap in hand, for additional borrowing authority.
The implications for the Canadian economy of such massive borrowing by the federal Government are as harmful as they are far reaching. The main problem for the Atlantic Provinces is that in the years ahead exorbitantly high interest payments on the national debt will leave little budgetary room for stimulative measures designed to resuscitate the crippled economy of the region.
In particular, I ask how the Government will find the $500 million that the Kirby Report says is needed for a complete restructuring of the Atlantic fishery. Clearly the state of the fishery on the East Coast is the single most urgent problem faced by the four Atlantic Provinces since World War II. Unless it is resolved, we in the Atlantic Provinces, all four Provinces alike, will continue to be forced to be wards of the federal Government, reduced to living from hand to mouth on the strength of transfer payments to provincial Governments and individuals.
Throughout the Atlantic region, the fishery has a potential work force of something like 100,000 people, about half engaged in the fish processing plants and the other half engaged in the actual catch. Much of the potential, however, is not being realized because the industry is literally on its knees. The fishing season is upon us and a black cloud hangs over those trying to eke out a meagre living from what was once a thriving concern.
The immediate challenge, of course, is to rationalize the small handful of major fish plants that employ the bulk of the
50,000	workers in the fish processing part of the industry. For example, H. B. Nickerson and Sons Ltd., which is of vital importance to Prince Edward Island because of its Georgetown Seafoods plant, at one point had a work force of some 10,000 people. In fact, in Georgetown alone, in that one plant, some 300 full-time jobs were eliminated when the doors were closed in the Fall of 1982. When part-time workers are taken into account, as many as 570 jobs were at stake.
I have been pleading with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) and the Government as a whole to help revive Georgetown Seafoods. But those pleas have fallen largely on deaf ears.
Now I would be the first to admit, Sir, that the plant's problems cannot be resolved, cannot be dealt with or addressed, and should not be, in isolation from any over-all
Borrowing Authority
strategy for the Atlantic fishery. By the same token, however, the plant's difficulties should not be totally ignored while a broader solution is being pursued. In fact, the major obstacle to the reopening of Georgetown Seafoods is the lack of high quality fish supplies required for processing and for making the plant profitable. Only a more generous fish quota from the federal Government-and the federal Government is the one with authority in this respect-is keeping Georgetown Seafoods from once more playing an important role in the Island's economy. But in response to overtures from myself and my colleague, the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass), and from the P.E.I. Government for such increased access to fish supplies in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, the federal Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) has stubbornly refused even to consider the proposal, arguing that it would dislocate supplies in other parts of the Atlantic region, especially in the Province of Nova Scotia. The Minister's concern is grossly misplaced, Mr. Speaker. The fact is that any assured fish quota for the Georgetown Seafoods plant, even if it involved a transfer of licences from Nickerson's to another operator, would not necessarily jeopardize fish supplies elsewhere in the region.
The Atlantic fishery, Sir, is on its knees. Fish processing plants are closing all over the region. Consequently, there is an oversupply of fish for procesing purposes. The Government has had the Kirby Report in its hands for many months, well beyond the point when it could justify procrastination and delay. The report was publicly released on February 17. The Deputy Prime Minister told me in the House, in Oral Question Period, on April 29, that the Government concurred with virtually all of Mr. Kirby's recommendations, including presumably those relating to the restructuring of the fish processing plants. If that is the case, why is action being delayed? Surely there has been ample time to consult with all concerned, among them the companies themselves, the banks, the respective provincial Governments and the workers.
If the fishery were instead located in Ontario and Quebec, central Canada in general, action would long since have been taken. The Government has hinted broadly that it may not be able to afford a master plan for the fishery in the current fiscal year, but it was able to come up with $200 million out of thin air within 24 hours to save what little was left of the reputation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in order to patch up the celebrated budgetary leak a few weeks ago. Why could that money not have been spent instead on the Atlantic fishery? The budget provides some money, I grant you that, to the fishery under general categories like Special Recovery Capital Projects. But as Mr. Kirby has rightly pointed out, what is needed is not a few dollars here and a few dollars there for a wharf or a vessel here or there or wherever; a total strategy designed to rebuild the fishery from the ground up is what is required. I urge the Government to recognize the fact and get on with the job.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that the task will be costly. On the other hand, the cost of not

May 26, 1983
Borrowing Authority
acting now in terms of lost output, lost wages and lost taxes on earned income would be even greater. If the federal Government still refuses to act, it should step aside and let someone else do the job. That is a message, Sir, which I think the Atlantic Provinces will doubtless send to Ottawa in the next federal election.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I enter this debate this afternoon, albeit for only ten minutes, on Bill C-151, an act respecting borrowing authority. In this Bill the Government is asking for a total of $14.7 billion. It used to be that we would talk around here in terms of "well, what's a million?" Today the buzz words are "what's a billion?" We all know that the cost of running a government and the country has increased substantially, but we on this side of the House constantly wonder whether or not those funds are being wisely spent.
This afternoon I would like to address very briefly one aspect of Government expenditure, that of national defence, and more specifically, the defence of our most northern reaches, the high Arctic. The reason I have chosen to zero in on this specific aspect of Government spending and the woefully inadequate aspect of Government expenditures for our defence in the far North is that I recently returned from a
13,000	kilometre trip in the High Arctic along with other Members of this House and European deputies and Members of Parliament who are members also of the North Atlantic Assembly. I was absolutely shocked to learn of the woefully inadequate defences that our country actually has in the far North when one considers the Soviet Union encompasses the whole eastern and far northern part of the High Arctic. I am not going to give a brief sabre rattling speech, but I just want to give you a few facts and statistics. Believe me, our European friends were more shocked than we were when we discovered some of the following figures and facts.
To begin with, the Government is at present engaged in negotiating the purchase of several hundred F-18A jet fighters.
I do not know why this country is involved in the purchase of jet fighters. We no longer have a raison d'etre, as it were, to be in that phase of defence or offence should a war occur, except in a very limited capacity in Europe within the NATO umbrella. But in North America we are dealing with ICBMs, and the Russians would have to have rocks in their heads to send manned bombers over the Arctic ice cap to bomb North America. 1 notice some of my Liberal friends are getting a little excited over there. They are still thinking in terms of the 1950s. Those jet fighters are going to cost us at least $5.5 billion. They will be totally useless for Arctic patrol. They cannot go any distance at all, whether it is in the High Arctic or in Europe. In the High Arctic there is no place for them to land. There are only three airfields in the entire far North, and I am speaking of well above the 60th parallel. Now, Mr. Speaker, this is $5.5 billion for a useless jet plane which cannot be used to defend our own country. I am not talking about NATO or the European theatre.
What have the Soviets got? They have six divisions, 400 warships and 600 aeroplanes, mainly for reconnaissance and surveillance. Against that, Mr. Speaker, we have a junior
ranking general at the brigadier level. We have the grand total of 75 people attached to National Defence in the High Arctic, of whom 42 are civilians. The rest are professional soldiers. In addition to that, we have several hundred Inuit and Indian scouts on a part-time basis. They perform a very valuable service in search and rescue, but really, as a fighting unit, with all due respect, they cannot be considered professional soldiers. Our Air Force in the far North consists of two planes, both of them Twin Otters, one of them seconded from the RCMP. Again, facing us across the polar ice cap: six Soviet divisions, 400 warships and 600 fighter airplanes.
The other aspect of our woefully undefended High Arctic is, of course, our relations with the United States. No one is anticipating an invasion from United States, granted. However, from an economic point of view and from the point of view of maintaining our sovereignty, it was not until 1969 that we even attempted to prove to the United States that we in fact controlled our High Arctic up to and including the North Pole and the polar ice cap. It is so bad, we learned from our military advisers in Yellowknife, that the Americans send their nuclear powered submarines through our territorial waters, under the polar ice cap, and when they return to the U.S. bases, only then do we give them permission for the journey that they have already made. This means that the Americans do not respect the longitudinal line that geographically divides the Yukon from Alaska as it is extended to the polar ice cap.
The reason the Americans refuse to accept this line and de facto, in effect, refuse to accept our sovereignty over the high North or the High Arctic is that the Prudhoe oil well basin comes down in a southeasterly direction and it does not extend in a northwesterly direction. The Americans know that much of that oil may very well fall under Canadian jurisdiction. So, for the time being, militarily, as a first step, the Americans are refusing to recognize the extension of the Yukon-Alaska border to the North Pole. Economically, that will of course be extremely important to Canada if and when we strike oil in the Beaufort Sea.
The Government is requesting $14.7 billion more, to borrow most of its money on the open market, I presume, and is proposing to spend at least $5.5 billion on the F-18A jet-fighter, which is of virtually no tactical use in North America in view of the fact that the Americans already have a massive interceptory jet-fighter presence in the United States, and in view of the fact that if the Soviets should attack Canada and the continental United States, it will not be from manned bombers of 1955 vintage but, rather, with ICBMs.
I really question the wisdom of borrowing $5.5 billion. Indeed, by the time we receive delivery of these planes, the capabilities and, in fact, safety of which are extremely questionable at the present time, the figure might well reach $7 billion or $8 billion, which would be half the $14.7 billion which Bill C-151 is asking the House to give the Government authority to borrow. In the next three or four years, half of that amount could conceivably go toward a jet-fighter which
May 26, 1983

we do not need, which is, tactically speaking, unnecessary in this part of the world. We all know very well that the Government should be spending money on reconnaissance and surveillance, hardware in the form of reconnaissance and surveillance planes and sea-based craft, such as submarines. That is our role within NORAD and within the purview of our own defence. It is not to spend $5 billion to $8 billion on jet-fighters when, at the present time, we have 75 military personnel in the North, two Twin-Otter planes, one of which is seconded to us from the RCMP, and a few Inuit and Indians attempting to scout for us, mainly in the area of search and rescue.
Therefore, on the one hand, in conventional surveillance and reconnaissance, we are woefully inadequate in the North, and on the other hand, the Government is proposing to waste $5 billion to $8 billion on tactical jet-fighters which we do not need and which cannot be deployed in the High Arctic.
1 notice, Mr. Speaker, that my allotted time has expired, and I appreciate the opportunity to make this intervention.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am deeply distressed, as I am sure many Canadians are also, that the Government has once again come forth to borrow more money, this time under the authority of Bill C-151, with very little thought given to the fact that the money must be squeezed out of the already hard-pressed Canadian taxpayers. To date, the Government has come to Parliament an unprecedented seven times in this session to ask Parliament for more and more money. In fiscal year 1982-83 alone, the Government came to Parliament four times to seek more and more money. At present, the Government already has borrowing authority for this fiscal year, 1983-84, for $16 billion.
Bill C-143 provided for $14 billion to be granted for fiscal year 1983-84, and for an extra $2 billion, which was slated for last year, to be carried over into this year. All in all, some $16 billion was already earmarked for the present fiscal year. Now, based on the Government's financial requirements of $26.7 billion, and existing borrowing authority of $16 billion which I just mentioned, the Government requires some $10.7 billion in additional borrowing authority for this year. However, the Bill which we are asked to pass is requesting $14.7 billion in new money, $4 billion more than is indicated by the national requirements of the $26.7 billion. Of this amount, it has been estimated that $2 billion does not have to be used this year, and may be carried forward into the future. What this really boils down to is that the Government not only has a cushion of $2 billion for this year, but it has also arranged for itself a further cushion of $2 billion to be used in any year.
I would also like to point out that there is really no urgency to the passage of this Bill, because the Government already has $16 billion in borrowing authority, as I have already indicated, which is more than enough to last for several months.
Spending taxpayer's dollars without due attention to priority by the Government, or by any person, is an act of irresponsibility and a violation of trust which should never be condoned.
Borrowing Authority
Further, the Government does not even follow its own guidelines of six and five, because spending for this year alone will be up some 12 per cent. What is even more calamitous is that spending by the Government has risen from 21 per cent of the Gross National Product four years ago to 26 per cent. When one adds all of this up, including the spending of all the provincial and municipal Governments across Canada, this figure is dangerously close to 50 per cent of the Gross National Product. When one takes into comparative consideration the figures for the United States of approximately 35 per cent to 36 per cent of their Gross National Product, one can readily see that the total public spending in Canada is completely out of hand, to the detriment of the private enterprise system which is being financially drained of its capacity to produce jobs and to increase production.
To emphasize this point further, in 1982, borrowing by the federal Government accounted for 51 per cent of all new security issues placed in Canada. Borrowing of that magnitude has a marked effect on the supply and demand for money and on the interest rates, again to the detriment of private enterprise. To make matters worse, the budget points to little by way of deficit reduction over the next four years. If this keeps up, there is no question but that the deficit will be in excess of $25 billion for each of the next four years.
The gross debt of the Government has risen from $134 billion as of March 31, 1982, to between $160 billion to $165 billion by March 31 of this year. However, this does not include the debts of the 306 Crown corporations and the money that is owed by Governments to the various pension funds. All in all, when everything is taken into consideration, the true debt of the Government is a staggering $262 billion to $265 billion, which works out to just about $11,000 for every man, woman and child in Canada.
I would ask, Mr. Speaker, what has happened to common sense? The taxpayers' pockets are not bottomless pits. There must be an end to this terrible injustice done to the people of Canada. What has happened to a responsible Government and to responsible spending by Governments in Canada? 1 believe that all Governments must come down from cloud nine and face the realities of this nation.
1 would also suggest that Ottawa in itself is a very poor example of what makes up Canada. I would suggest that the decision makers in this capital come down from their ivory towers, get out of Ottawa, and face the real Canada of two million unemployed, the real Canada of continuing high interest rates, the real Canada of people living on relief through no fault of their own and living on a subsistence allowance which is often less than what some bureaucrats charge to their expense accounts for an evening out on the town entertaining at Government expense.
That is the real Canada about which many people living in Ottawa know nothing and about which some care even less. Yet the Government ignores these realities and extracts more

May 26. 1983
Borrowing Authority
and more money from the taxpayers for more and more questionable spending.
I have no quarrel with productive and necessary spending on such things as old age pensions, medicare, hospitalization and other similar worth-while projects. I fully support those, but I draw the line at some questionable spending that has been going on. I have listed just a few examples that highlight the magnitude of these expenditures and provide instances of questionable spending on the part of the Government. 1 have drawn these examples from several sources including the annual reports from the Auditor General, Order Paper questions, newspaper articles and the Estimates.
We all know that bureaucrats have a reputation for being paper pushers. In 1981, the Department of Supply and Services purchased 12,600 metric tonnes of office paper at a cost of $17 million. That works out to roughly 90 pounds of office paper per public servant. Between March 1, 1980, and May 31, 1981, the Government gave out $3.5 million in taxi fares. The largest single bill from any Government Department was perhaps appropriately from Transport Canada, amounting to $422,000. At current Ottawa taxi rates of approximately $1.20 per mile, this is enough to go around the world about 100 times.
In fiscal year 1981-82, eleven Government Departments spent a total of $10.4 million on hospitality which includes food, booze and entertainment. That is the equivalent of
700,000	bottles of liquor. It is also only the tip of the iceberg since it only includes contracted hospitality where the total bill of a Department was greater than $25,000.
Between April 1, 1980 and June 30, 1981, the federal Government spent $674,972 to supply public servants with briefcases. Surely Government employees are paid enough to buy their own briefcases.
With the full blessing and knowledge of the CMHC President, CMHC paid $15,000 to defray the travel costs of employees participating in a staff hockey tournament in Toronto.
In February of 1981, the CNR spent $64,244 to purchase advertising space for wishing the CPR, its chief competitor, a happy birthday.
In 1978-79, the cost to CIDA of late and damaged food shipments was $1.5 million. To date, spending by the federal Government on the metric conversion program exceeds $65 million. Last year alone the Metric Commission spent $12.4 million.
During the 1981 postal strike the Metric Commission spent $12 to send a 14-page metric cookbook by air courier to a Winnipeg woman. In 1981, two TV chefs-Bruno Gerussi and Madame Benoit-were given a six-week TV contract worth $110,000 to promote metric cooking. This list goes on and on.
On the day that the Post Office became a Crown corporation, the Government helped employees celebrate by providing $300,000 of taxpayers' money for free coffee, doughnuts and souvenir envelopes.
In July, 1981, the Post Office spent $200,000 to run advertisements in 39 newspapers and publications to tell Canadians that postal service will improve in the future. One would think that improved service would speak for itself.
Janet Smith, an assistant secretary to the Cabinet, was sent to Nice in southern France for four months to learn French. The cost to the taxpayer of this Riviera education was $12,000 plus Ms. Smith's salary which is in the range of $60,000 to $70,000 per year. I can go on and on.

system which the Minister has now concluded cost $24 million.
1 still maintain that it cost a lot more than that.
1 have a list of these consultants. I would like to read them into the record but that would take too long. Let the record simply show that all 25 are in this list. Again, I believe that there were probably more than 25 consultants used when one learns the whole story.
We are also disturbed by the way money is wasted, even under the guise of worth-while projects. I can talk about our own region of Atlantic Canada, Mr. Speaker. The replacement of the old ferry Abegwait, which has been probably taken in the past from Borden, P.E.I. to Tormentine, N.B. cost $100 million. It is beyond any shadow of a doubt that CN Marine needlessly spent about $100 million. The old vessel was quite good and seaworthy and, in many ways, a better vessel than the new one of the same name. If $2 million or $3 million were spent on that vessel it would have provided good service for another ten years. Just think of what we could have done with that kind of saved money in Atlantic Canada.
Of course I could go on for hours relating such horror stories. In passing let me mention another story to which allusion has been made today. It is the $125 million spent on a project of which the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) is very familiar since he was very instrumental in it, the celebrated Consolidated Computer debacle. In that case $125 million of taxpayers' money went right down the drain.
While it is not particularly positive, I would like to trace how our image in the world has gone down as our economic capabilities have declined. There was an interesting feature in a recent issue of Time magazine which described how our influence in the United Nations has become that of a bit player. We now have a walk-on part, when Canada once had an influence that was disproportionate to our population, disproportionate because we had the capability, the respect and the capacity to do great things on the world scene. What has happened to us since 1968? Canada's position has declined steadily. Anyone who wants to look at the OECD statistics- you need not believe me-will see that right now Canada is last in terms of the industrialized nations of the West. Why has this occurred? I think it has occurred largely because of economic mismanagement. The results of that economic mismanagement we see here today. The Government wants more and it has to come to Parliament to borrow money which, as the previous speaker said, is not really needed. If this Bill goes through, the Government will have an extra $2 billion to play with, almost as much as the Government is going to spend on professional and special services this year. This is very bad for economic development. I do not understand why this Government continues to abuse the priorities that made this country great.
The Hon. Member for Brant in his previous speech pointed out the ridiculous situation that exists in our North, one of the greatest storehouses of wealth, treasure and pride that any country in the world could possibly have. But we cannot even
Borrowing Authority
patrol it. We are reduced to using native people, who have the skills to be trackers, to provide the kinds of services which other nations have provided by military means, electronic surveillance and things like that. We are reduced to almost frontier Daniel Boone or Davy Crockett techniques in the twentieth century to patrol our own North. We do not have the money to improve the situation. Even the wealthiest nation in the world, the United States with its large internal market, has made some tough choices. By contrast, countries like ours which have placed their faith in unrestrained deficit spending and socialist policies are having extreme problems. We do not have to look very far to see the results.
Recently the great nation of France elected a socialist government. Now its President, President Mitterrand, is reaping the benefits of his particular socialist policies, which have a startling resemblance to the policies this Government has been prescribing for our country. Francois Mitterrand came into power on the basis that France was going to spend its way to prosperity. What does France have now? It has monetary and currency controls, and the freedom of French citizens to take vacations has been curtailed. There are riots in the streets and there is talk about some of their more radical elements beseiging Parliament.
Let us take a look at Michael Foote, the Opposition leader in the United Kingdom. He has espoused all sorts of socialist policies, again similar to the policies which this Liberal Government, under the guise of asking free enterprise to be the engine of economic recovery, is foisting off on this country. What has happened in Great Britain? The Prime Minister, Mrs. Thatcher, has made hard choices for the U.K. She has reduced inflation and put a sense of pride and priority back in that nation. She is ahead in the public opinion polls by an unprecedented lead as the British approach their upcoming election. The socialist opposition is once more having difficulty and obviously will go down to defeat.
Why cannot Canada learn from the experiences of our neighbours? I cannot understand why not. 1 know it is trite in this House to quote cliches and homilies from the past, even though I maintain it is useful, Sir, but if they did not have some intrinsic value they would not have survived.
Let me put a few passages on the record from the statements of a great American president, Abraham Lincoln. He has been noted in the past for uttering the odd word of wisdom. Some of his prescriptions for national development are as follows:
You cannot bring about prosperity by discouraging thrift. You cannot help the wage earner by pulling down the wage payer. You cannot establish sounder security on borrowed money. You cannot keep out of trouble by spending more than you earn.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that you are signalling to tell me that my allotted time has expired. That is a pity because 1 would have liked to have put more of Abraham Lincoln's philosophy on the record. Certainly my friends opposite would benefit from reading them.

Mr. Speaker, I am especially pleased to follow the Hon. Member

May 26. 1983
Borrowing Authority
for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) in this debate. Many things that affect his contituency also affect mine. We are neighbours and we attempt to work together over and over again to be of assistance to the constituents of northern Nova Scotia. One of the facts of life, as I see it, as much as I object to this borrowing Bill, is the gigantic sums of money that will be taken out of the free market system. This will do two things. First, it will take away money that could be used by free enterprise to inject the economy in a productive way and to provide the employment required that we do not have. Second, there is a real danger that interest rates which have slowly declined are going to escalate once more because of the tremendous interference in the money markets by the central Government. This takes away potential funds that would be available at more sensible interest rates to small business and medium sized business, the real effective backbone of this country. These business people are the people who produce the jobs that would eliminate the unemployment problem facing us today.
Right now we have an unprecedented rate at which home building grants have been requested. This has happened because of lower interest rates and because of a re-evaluation by the Canadian public which has created new confidence. Instead of the Government using additional funds to assist those new home owners to build the homes that will provide the jobs-the home building industry is the best indicator of the degree of prosperity that will exist-what does the Government do? Because of its intransigence and insensitivity to the individual Canadian, no more funds are available. Indeed, for a period of time the Government initially said it would. Assistance to prospective new home owners and the home building industry would be the greatest single stimulus we have to help this nation pull out of this recession. We do not have that.
In Atlantic Canada, the Maritimes and in many parts of Quebec we are still in a very deep recession. The one thing 1 have found out in the time I have served in this House is that even when we are coming out of a recession we, in Atlantic Canada, experience it last. Usually we need an extra degree of stimulation to catch up with the rest of the country that starts enjoying the new prosperity that happens following a recession.
One of the sad things about this Government and its insensitivity to our part of Canada is that we see no new capital works projects of any significance. We had the Minister from Nova Scotia, the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) come to Halifax. Rather than trying to produce some industrial infrastructure for Halifax to stimulate the building of new industry, what does he do? He announces that he is going to build another office building to interfere with the private sector. If additional office space is required in Halifax, the private sector will produce it.

But what does the Minister say? He says, "We are going to build a new office building". This is to be built on a piece of land which the federal Government does not even own. In other words, the federal Government is trying to take
a piece of land from the provincial Government that could be used for industrial purposes to put up an office building which will be in competition with office building owners in the private sector who would be quite willing and able to produce new office space, if that is what is required. That is the insensitivity of this Government to our area and the difficulties we face.
The Government wants to take money out of the money market and run a deficit in excess of the six and five it is asking public servants to accept over a two year period as increases in their incomes. The new spending estimates for this year are running something like the 11 per cent in one year that the Government is asking public servants to accept as increases in their salaries over two years. Members of the House of Commons are faced with a situation where they are not in a position to give their office staff even a 1 per cent increase because of the passage of the Bill which put the six and five in place. Some people wonder why there is bad morale on Parliament Hill. The Government's insensitivity to the people who work here is the best example.
We hear talk about the things the Government will do for our areas. At the same time we are facing a cut in the transportation subsidy available to our businessmen upon whom the Government relied to move their products to central Canada. What will the Government do with that subsidy? It will cut it by 10 per cent. It will try to eliminate it altogether and put us in the position where we were after World War I when we were nothing more than the captive market of central Canada.
I say to western Members of Parliament, who are now thinking about allowing the Government to do something with the Crowsnest Pass rate, to use Atlantic Canada as an example of what happens when one gives away something that is one's birthright, as were the Maritime freight rates to Atlantic Canada. What happened? We found out that the Government sold us a bill of goods, and just when things started to happen, it pulled the rug out from under us. I say to western Members that the Crow rates are a birthright of the people of western Canada. Canadians gave tremendous advantages to the railways of the country which made CP one of the largest multinational companies in the world. I say that we should let the railways work under the Crowsnest Pass rate from here to eternity. I say to western Canadians that they should never give away what they have to bureaucrats, especially to Government Members across the way who will tell them one thing today and something else tomorrow.
The Crow rates should be protected. Every Member of the House, regardless of where he comes from, should tell the railways to work out some other scheme. I say to the Government that if the railways figure they are being shortchanged by the Crow rate, they should work out a scheme whereby they can present evidence to Canadians that they are not being paid the equivalent of the difference between the Crowsnest Pass rates and their actual costs. Also I say that they should pay

them out of the general revenues of Canada but keep on the statute books forever the Crowsnest Pass rates. It was a special deal given to western Canadians. It was to entice people to go to western Canada, to entice people to farm and to grow wheat and other grains in western Canada. That is what made our country great today. I ask Members from western Canada to stand firm and fight against any tinkering with these rates. If they do not, they will get the same double deal as we in Atlantic Canada got as far as the Maritime Freight Rates Act was concerned. Tomorrow they will discover that they are not able to sell their wheat because the federal Government has shoved up the prices of wheat so that we are no longer competitive with the other great wheat growing nations of the world.
Those are just some of my concerns about this borrowing Bill and some of the ways in which I think we might be able to do something that would be advantageous to the people of Canada, especially the people of Atlantic Canada.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to put a few remarks on the record regarding another proposed borrowing by the Government. I think most Members of the House are aware of the rather
Borrowing Authority
unusual and somewhat immoral borrowing practices of the group across the floor. With Bill C-l 11 just less than a year ago, the Liberals borrowed $6.6 billion. With Bill C-l25 last July, they borrowed another $7 billion. With Bill C-l28 they borrowed another $4 billion in November. Will Bill C-l43 they borrowed another $19 billion just over a month ago. Now they come before the House to borrow another $14.7 billion. This accounts, in just 11 months, for $51.3 billion. 1 think the House should look quite carefully at the matter this time. The Government comes before us with $16 billion in borrowing authority still available to it.
According to its budget, which was brought down only a few weeks ago, it estimated a $26.7 billion deficit. The amount proposed here, combined with the existing borrowing authority which is still available, means that the amount of deficit listed in the budget will be exceeded by an additional $4 billion. Once these kinds of amounts are being borrowed ahead of time and we have bureaucrats from the Department of Finance telling the public that they are just for a contingency fund, we have to start informing Canadians and looking inside ourselves to see just what exactly is the Government's plan. Some people say that it is patronage. Some people say that it is slush. Some people say that it is a pork barrel. But the Government's own record demonstrates its inability to spend the dollars of Canadian taxpayers appropriately.
I would like to put a few examples of this on the record. A recent one was Consolidated Computer with $100 million down the tube. There has never been a proper parliamentary investigation into it. It has never really been revealed as to who in the chain of command was responsible or the kinds of firings that would be appropriate. Then we had Candu. I am glad to see the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) in the House. We know that the Candu program is running into continued rough times. It is continuing to write off more than $100 million per year just on its heavy water production. Our recent customer, of course, is Argentina. Its head of state is on record as publicly saying that he wants the Candu reactor program to continue so that Argentina can make atomic weapons, perhaps to use against Great Britain or even against Canada. Who knows whether or not we would be drawn into the Falklands conflict?
The Cruise is another example of where the Government has gone to seed. The majority of Canadian public opinion is opposed to it, but because of some desire to have more credible links with the White House and the Pentagon, the Government is dragging us along on that. As the former speaker mentioned, now there is the proposed Crow change where the Government, through the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), is trying to describe the position of the New Democratic Party as reactionary. Of course we have some concern about the position of the Tories on this. We have some Tories who are for it and some who are against it. It should be clear that what

May 26, 1983
Borrowing Authority
is being proposed by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Transport will certainly not help farmers on the Prairies. The Minister of Agriculture knows that by 1990 it will take at least $1 billion out of the farming communities on the Prairies. These are dollars which will simply not stay there. These are dollars which will not go into the purchase of new machinery or new equipment. These are dollars that will not go in the form of municipal taxes for road upgrading, so everybody has to rubberhaul and so on. Yet Government Members, the few it has who will travel west of Ontario, are saying that the NDP position is reactionary and will stop the movement of all kinds of commodities.
The fact of the matter is that we have proposed the only sensible way to deal with any kind of rail line upgrading, that is, to pay the difference between the Crow and the real costs to the railroads for grain and other commodity movement to their point of exit from Canada and to take Canadian tax dollars to pay for the actual upgrading. However, to change the Crow is ridiculous. That is the sleeper in that Bill, along with the sleeper on the Dominion coal blocs.
I am not going to spend a lot of time speaking on the record of the Liberals because they will not be the Government very much longer. 1 am worried that there may be a minority Tory Government and we will have some trouble keeping them in line. Perhaps Canadians will come to their senses and elect the NDP in the next federal election. Perhaps they will do so as a result of a few of the remarks I want to make. We do not get to hear any Liberals speaking in the House. They rely on their flacks and hacks upstairs with the machinery to put the glint on everything and then put it out on the street and try and make it saleable. The Party is so unsalvageable now, the flacks and hacks are beginning to head for cover knowing there will be a change in Government fairly soon.
The Hon. Member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) made some interesting comments. He said the Government of France is in great difficulty because it is a socialist government. What he tried to focus on in that case was exchange controls, particularly related to people travelling outside the country on holiday. The Hon. Member for Central Nova should recall, since he likes to rely so frequently and heavily on Americans, that his idealogical predecessors, Richard Nixon and Lyndon Johnson, brought in exchange controls in the United States, something the Tories do not like to talk about too often.
1 want to deal with the relevance of his argument with regard to Margaret Thatcher's lead in the polls. That is because of the way she is taking food out of the mouths of children. Many people in this world are aware of that kind of reactionary politics of taking milk money away from families with school-aged children who cannot afford to provide milk for their children. That is where a pretty good chunk of the funds in terms of cutting those kinds of social programs came from for Mrs. Thatcher and her Party. I seriously hope that the Brits show a little more sense in the coming election than
to re-elect the "iron lady" who has laid all over the working people in that country.
I would like to talk about what 1 see as the main difficulty with the Liberal-Tory policy. I think the Liberals waste more than the Tories would, but it is hard to know because we have not had a chance to observe them in action for more than two decades. The Liberals have a tendency to throw money at things rather than having any kind of industrial plan or a plan that involves the workers and small business people. The Tories are always saying that if you only give private enterprise a chance, away it will go. An example of free enterprise failing to operate is B.C. Timber in my area. Prince Rupert was shut down. The operations in Terrace were shut down, as well as The Nass, Kitwanga and over into the Hazeltons where Rim Products is still down.
What does the Government come in with? The Tories say to leave them alone, they will come back to life, don't worry about the fact that all these communities are dying. That is what you get with free enterprise, a lot of dead communities all over the place. What do the Liberals do? They use a new kind of right-to-work legislation which is called NEED, FLIP, JET, all Government programs that are supposed to salvage the communities. They are, of course, short-term. They get everybody up on their feet again. They really are right-to-work. However, what it does is effectively to lower the wages being paid to those working on these sites. It effectively destroys the concept of collective bargaining, or at least makes it much more difficult in many of those communities where literally thousands of workers are out because of this "free enterprise".
I want to say that this is another sleazy attempt by the Government to borrow money when it does not even need the money. It still has S16 billion. It wants to slip this through so that if it has to go to a quick election in the Fall, it will have a little bit of pork to throw around.
It is about time there was some kind of intelligent approach to expenditures. There should be a certain amount of statutory expenditures for social programs, and all Parties should work to keep those safety nets and social programs in place. The important money should be put forward to encourage co-ops, worker-owned and operated industries. We have seen the problems private enterprise gets into when it does not go out and find adequate markets, as with B.C. Timber. It should be going into panel board, chipboard, paper, furniture and other items. That will only come if the local communities are given the opportunity and some support, technical, R and D and financial, to re-tool and re-finance those industries to make them locally owned.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on Bill C-151. It brings back memories of the Liberal platform in the 1980 election. They were going to be all things to all people. What have we seen? They asked the people for their confidence, that they will lead them to the Promised Land, and everything else. This is a complete reversal. It has been nothing but downhill and borrowing all the way.
May 26, 1983

This budget, were it tabled when the polls showed the Liberals in an advantageous electoral position, would be called an election budget. This borrowing authority Bill will provide the pork barrel, as mentioned by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) used to finance the next election, whenever it comes. I want to say this: the people will not be fooled as easily as they were before.
I will deal with the summer student program because it affects my riding to a great extent. There was an allocation of a further $70 million in addition to the $170 million already allocated to try to beef up the unemployment situation with respect to students across Canada. In my constituency of Victoria-Haliburton, last year we received $151,876 in funds for this program. The formula devised for the allocation of funds this year was based on a survey of the student surplus rate in each constituency. This survey, taken last summer, indicated that only 358 students were unemployed in my riding. I am not sure who did the survey, but I can assure Hon. Members that that figure bears no relation to reality. The method used in conducting the survey varies from riding to riding.
There was a great discrepancy with regard to rural ridings. My riding is 150 miles east and west and close to 150 north and south. There is a manpower Outreach office in Halibur-ton, a manpower office in Peterborough, one in Lindsay, one in Oshawa and one in Newmarket. Students in rural Ontario do not have the facilities nor the funds to travel to the manpower offices. They know perfectly well that there is no work for them. Why should they travel 100 or more miles to a manpower office to be told, "We will take your name and if something comes up, we will let you know"? This formula was wrong for determining the number of students unemployed in a riding such as mine.
I have appealed the additional allocation of only $4,194 to the Minister, but as yet I have not had a reply. It is unbelievable that neighbouring constituencies have received thousands of additional dollars. Why is that? They are close to a manpower office. There is no problem for the students there to register. It is a totally different situation from the one in my riding.
If this survey is upheld, the additional funding in the budget will not be seen in my riding, even though we have applications this year for well over $500,000 on an allocation of only $156,100. Obviously, judging by these figures, the additional $4,000 funding is welcome and is most needed, but it will be only a drop in the bucket. The $100 million allocated to the Farm Credit Corporation will be helpful only to a few farmers, those who are really in distress. When you realize the depth to which farmers are in debt, you quickly see that $100 million will not go very far in this day and age. The change in loss carry-over rules will help the struggling farmer, but it will do little to help those who are in dire straits and cannot get any of this $100 million. The expansion of the role of the Federal Business Development Bank may or may not be of assistance to farmers. Details in the budget are quite sketchy as to
Borrowing Authority
exactly how the role of the Federal Business Development Bank may be expanded.
1 want to say something about Government institutions and how their employees treat farmers. I may say that 1 personally have experienced this treatment when speaking on behalf of my constituents to some of the managers of the Federal Business Development Bank. I want to tell you at this time, Mr. Speaker, that their attitude was less than co-operative, and yet these civil servants are there to serve the people. Their attitude could be a little better, and I have been very disappointed especially by the attitude of one manager whom 1 personally contacted on behalf of a very sincere, dedicated business within the farming community. I was more or less told that the affair was none of my business, but this businessman eventually got the money. I do not want to go into detail about how he received the money, but he received the money from the Federal Business Development Bank. There probably was a change in the people who were dealing with his specific application. Now, this should not happen. This did not happen on only one occasion, and I think that this is something that the Minister in charge should probably look into. This is just not the way people should be treated when they go to a Government office.
The Government's intention to remove the Canadian ownership special charge in respect of companies was merely a formality. 1 do not think that anyone expected the Government to remove this tax even after Petrofina and Dome had been paid for. It is, however, an additional tax that was originally to have been of limited duration. Yet another new 6 per cent tax has been added on probably in order to pay for cable TV and Pay TV.
Related to what I said a few moments ago regarding Dome and Petrofina, let us look at the gasoline tax situation. Approximately a week ago, we in Ontario saw a gasoline price war. Gasoline was selling for 25.6 cents per litre. The price of gasoline went down as low as 24.6 cents or 24.5 cents per litre, but today at the same pumps this gasoline is selling for 45.6 cents per litre. This can be seen here in the City of Ottawa, it can be seen any place in Ontario. This is a 20 cent difference in the price of a litre of gasoline.
What does the price of gasoline do to inflation in our economy? The price of gasoline in this day and age is probably one of the biggest creators of inflation in the cost of productivity, and hurts the tourist industry and probably every sector of the economy. Why is there such a discrepancy in the price of gasoline, a discrepancy of 20 cents a litre? I have put this question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) in the House of Commons before. The Minister has never really given me an answer; he just skates around the question. The tourist industry is a big industry in Canada today and it is especially big in my area, and one of the biggest deterrents to the tourist industry is the difference between the cost of gasoline per litre or per gallon in Canada and the cost of gasoline in the United States.

May 26, 1983
Borrowing Authority
The second deterrent to the tourist industry is the Government tax on the cost of beverages. I do not argue whether or not beverages, as we know it in the tourist industry today, are needed. It is something which is there and it is there to stay, my friends, and it is something which plays a big part in bringing tourists to our country.
Then we may move to the field of accommodation as well. These are all services which are greatly affected by the Government tax here and the Government tax there. I will conclude in just a moment, Mr. Speaker, if you will give me a second. The Government is very, very prone to imposing a tax here and a tax there in order to raise money that is ill-spent. Thank you very much for your patience, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me no great pleasure to rise again to discuss another borrowing Bill. Not too long ago, the Government came before the House to ask permission to borrow money under a previous Bill. Bill C-151 seeks the aproval of the House to borrow $14.7 billion. This, Mr. Speaker, is almost an unbelieveable amount of money in view of the fact that the Government has come before this session of Parliament with the same request seven times. It came before Parliament under Bill C-30 to borrow $12 billion, under C-59 to borrow $14 billion, under Bill C- 111 to borrow $6.6 billion, under Bill C-125 to borrow $7 billion, under Bill C-128 to borrow $4 billion, under Bill C-143 to borrow $19 billion, and now the Government is seeking to borrow $14.7 billion. That is a total of $61.6 billion, an unbelieveable amount of money to be borrowed in one session of Parliament.
This year's deficit as forecast by the Government will be approximately $31.3 billion, but can we believe that figure in view of the changes that have been made over the past year? I believe that we all recall the $200 million which was tacked on to the budget so that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) could squeeze out from under the allegation that he had leaked some of the provisions in the budget. In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, the Government has said that its financial requirements are $26.7 billion, and yet, as of April 1 this year, it had $16 billion in unused borrowing capacity, which means that it really needs to borrow $10.7 billion. However, the Minister has told us that he needs a cushion of $2 billion this year just in case. He does not really tell us what "just in case" means. Then he wants a surplus of another $2 billion next year "just in case", and again we do not know what that means. But we do have a clue that perhaps there will be a run on the Canadian dollar. That does not augur well for any of us. If the Government has to borrow money in the case of a run on the Canadian dollar, then we will be in desperate trouble over the next year.
I believe that it can be said without any exaggeration, Mr. Speaker, that the Government's expenditures are out of control. I do not think that it really knows how much the deficit will be this year. I do not think that it really knows about or has planned for a true expenditure plan. In effect, the Government is just hoping. It is hoping that the American economy will turn around sufficiently to pick up the Canadian economy.
The Government's expenditures boggle the imagination, Mr. Speaker. We are told that it spent $6 million each on two water bombers for the Yukon, and of course the fire season in the Yukon occurs at a time when ice covers most of the lakes. We would like to know what the Government are going to use the water bombers for. Perhaps they will be used to take Liberal Cabinet Ministers to the Yukon on fishing trips. As we get closer to the election, we will need to have these little handouts just in case they do not come back.
We heard in committee just recently, Mr. Speaker, about some of the wasteful expenditures of the Canadian International Development Corporation. Last year, the Government of one of the developing nations asked for an advance of $20,000 against a loan that it would be receiving from the Canadian Government. Did the Canadian Government give it the $20,000? Of course not. It gave that country $250,000, and no one knows why. The acting Deputy Minister says, "We don't have an answer". Last year over $8 million was allocated in such a manner. The record goes on and on and on. Petro-Canada, the window on the oil industry, has investment capital of somewhere around $7 billion, and last year had earnings of $10 million. That is unbelievable. This oil company is supposedly in the private sector yet it is wrapped up in bureaucracy. Perhaps this is speculation, Mr. Speaker, but it would not surprise me if one of the greatest scandals in this country in the next five to ten years will be the way the Government has operated Petro-Canada.
How did we arrive at this stage of excess, uncontrolled expenditure by the Government, with one hand not knowing what the other is doing? For the answer we must go back and consider a number of things. First, there is the National Energy Program. No one really believes that the National Energy Program ever did any good. One does not just have to read the newspapers; one can easily tell by talking to the bankers and investment people in many parts of the world. I have visited England, Germany and the United States in the last three months, and people there all repeat the same thing. They have told the Government their opinion, but Government Members would not repeat that in the House. They have said, "If you want investment capital in Canada, get rid of the National Energy Program, get rid of FIRA." The Government knows this.

Canadians would be interested in the situation we have here because they know full well the crime of taxation. They know full well that the promises of today usually end up as the taxes of tomorrow. Canadian taxpayers and small and medium-sized businessmen know that today's deficits are going to be the taxes of tomorrow. Canadians have become accustomed to the fact that the Government adjusts its economic forecasting almost every three months.
Over the last two years we have gone from a projected deficit of $11 billion to $19.8 billion; that is almost double. And that was just a miscalculation, Mr. Speaker.
For people who do know what a billion dollars is, Mr. Speaker, I can tell them that it is 1,000 million dollars, which would make a stack of one dollar bills about 85 miles high. At one time there was a Member of this House who said, "What's a million?" It was a large sum of money when the Government took over power. I say "took over power" because there is no longer any power with the Canadian people or with Parliament. That has all been usurped by the Government. When these people took over, the total spending authority that the Government used to lay before Parliament was about one-third of what it is now running in deficits alone. The deficit went from $11 billion to $19 billion to $24 billion, and it is projected now at $31 billion. One could say, "So what, we live in difficult economic circumstances. We have entered into all kinds of social contracts from which we cannot extricate ourselves. The Unemployment Insurance bill this year is $12 billion and there are of course statutory arrangements with the Provinces where the federal Government is locked in, and these agreements cannot be renegotiated. There is another way to pay back borrowed money rather than raising taxes later on. You can pay it back through inflation. That is the great con game which governments of this type have become accustomed to and comfortable with throughout the world. Spend money today, water down the currency, and pay your debts with watered down dollars. Not only are governments like that cheating themselves, they are really cheating the old age pensioners and people on fixed incomes who rely on governments for their sustenance. They are being paid in watered down dollars. When the currency is

Mr. Speaker, if I remember correctly, you came into the House about the same time that I did, that is, in 1972. Well, I stand to be corrected, but anyway, in 1972, as you will remember because you were here at that time, we had a minority Government. That was the time when the Government started to get into trouble because, as I understand, prior to that time the federal Government had a surplus of approximately $700 million. That was in 1970. In order for that minority Government to stay in power for as long as it did, and it lasted two years, it had to respond to the wishes and kicks of the NDP. That is where we started to go wrong. Then, of course, the problem escalated until the Auditor General, in approximately 1978, made the statement that to all intents and purposes Government expenditures were out of control.
1 believe that to be true, Mr. Speaker. I do not think that even today the Government has the public purse under control. In fact, I was speaking to an individual not so long ago who made the comment that unfortunately the Government is not aware that it does not have control of the purse strings. This is where the danger comes in. If we do not do something very quickly, we are going to create the situation where we are going to have a financial collapse. Consider our total debt, including provincial debt. It increased last year approximately $35 billion. We cannot stand that, Mr. Speaker. The total debt of the Third World is somewhere in the vicinity of $700 billion, and yet here we are in Canada with a debt of about one third of that amount. Certainly that is a disastrous situation to find ourselves in.
The worst part of it all is that this year the Government will increase that amount, possibly up to $35 billion, and it will probably be the same next year. How long can we stand that? Surely the members of Government should have enough basic business knowledge and understanding to know that the Government cannot continue along those lines. Surely they must realize that Government is the biggest business we have in Canada today, and that the guidelines which must be followed by any successful businesses in our communities must be applied to the federal Government. This is not happening. This is the part that concerns me. For instance, as I said earlier, this year it will cost us $18 billion just to pay the interest alone. If one uses one's mathematics, one will find that that amounts to $2 a day for every man, woman and child living in Canada. Every Canadian should realize upon rising in the morning that the first two dollars each person makes must go to pay for this interest cost.
May 26, 1983

So much of our funding is going without any return. Take, for instance, payment of interest. We do not make any financial gain from that. There is no productivity. The Government is placing a heavier load, as each successive year goes by on our people, on our Canadian taxpayer, on our business community. Actually, it is killing the goose that laid the golden egg, and yet it does not seem to realize it. Unless a change is made very soon, we will find far too much of the productivity of our country going simply to finance the debt. There does not seem to be any inclination on the part of any Hon. Members opposite to stop that.
Some years ago I was flabbergasted when the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, the Hon. Otto Lang, brought in the stabilization program for the western Canadian grain producer. It was set up in such a manner that the farmer, the producer, paid his dollar into the fund and the Government was to pay its $2 into the fund. I would have thought that it was a fair, honest and straightforward way to set up any program. However, what happened shortly there after? Your Honour will remember that Mr. Lang brought in another piece of legislation providing that the Government did not have to put in its $2. It would calculate it and keep it as a paper figure; but it would pay interest on it. However, somewhere along the line, there must be a payout. Otherwise, the program will not do the job for which it was intended. So what will happen? Next year, in our Estimates, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) will probably have to be responsible, a pretty substantial payout to the western grain producer will be necessary because of the fact that we are now going through times of extremely low prices. This is the irony of the whole situation.
In 1970 there was a surplus in the budget. These 12 or 13 years have been good years to us, except perhaps for the last two or three years. Those were the times when the Government should have been building up a balance in the bank. However, what did it do? Each successive year it went further and further into debt. What will happen now? Suppose that in 1984 or 1985 the economic cycle makes a turnaround. It is said that it makes a turnaround every 50 to 60 years. If Hon. Members opposite would remember, it is now just exactly 50 years from the 1930s. Now we are going into a down cycle and must pay off the tremendous debt. It will put a tremendously heavy load on our children and our grandchildren. However, there does not seem to be any thought concerning this matter. That is my concern.
What is the Government doing during these good years, by exploding the budget to this extent? It is unbelievable, the way it is exploding. For instance, last year when the budget was presented to us, it was supposedly to be just a bit over $10 billion; but it ended up being $25 billion or $26 billion. We do not have the final figures. However, it will be somewhere between those figures. Then, of course, as the Minister said, next year there will be a deficit of $31 billion. Are we to have
Borrowing Authority
another escalation of $16 billion? That would put it up in the $47 billion bracket, if that holds true.
Certainly, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) mentioned, and also my colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary North (Mr. Wright), a part of the problem was the National Energy Program. It is true that the Government saw some bucks out there and wanted to get its hands on the money, and it did. It took a few hundred million dollars out of the system. However, what has happened now? The chickens have come home to roost because of the fact that this year it is estimated that there will be a $6 billion payout on refunds on income tax alone, simply because the oil energy business has been cut back.
I could go on with other figures and show Your Honour where the Government is going wrong, but hopefully some Hon. Members opposite will be wise enough to see what the Government is doing to our country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome this opportunity to speak today with regard to the borrowing legislation, because it gives me an opportunity to put on the record my concerns over the economic policy, the taxation policy, of the Government. When we consider the borrowing Bill, we really must not look only at the numbers. Certainly, the numbers involved in the Bill are enough to impress anyone. The number of times the Government has come before the House to borrow are impressive in and of themselves. However, the real question upon which we must focus our attention is: What is the purpose of all of this borrowing? What kind of policies have led to this present situation? What are the values, the fundamental priorities of the Government when it comes to borrowing?
I think I would feel much better about this borrowing request if I thought it related to meeting the needs of people and to providing employment for Canadians. However, if we consider what is going on in the country, if we take a brief look at the budget which the Government introduced and which was recently passed through the House, we find that there is double-digit unemployment in Canada. We find the fact that the budget has accepted unemployment of 12.4 per cent for this year and unemployment of 11.4 per cent for next year. It even made predictions that after recovery, after a number of years, the best we could hope for would be to bring unemployment down to 7 per cent or 8 per cent.
In this context, it is very difficult to accept the notion that this borrowing will continue for the purpose of putting people back to work, because it is clear that the economic and manpower policies of the Government have failed to put Canadians back to work. The Government has, in fact, accepted a level of unemployment in this country which, until today, was unheard of. This is unprecedented in terms of a Government accepting such a level without really facing up to the problem and making a commitment to do something about it. So there is no way we can justify this borrowing by saying that the Government has turned its effort toward employment creation.

May 26, 1983
Borrowing Authority
I might approve of this borrowing if I thought it would improve equality in the country. For example, if the money were used to bring about greater equality between men and women in the Public Service I would be in favour of its expenditure. We know from a recent report that was made public and tabled recently that the gap between the wages of men and women in the Public Service has increased by some 12 per cent between last year and this year. That is a direct result of legislation brought into the House by the Government. The Government's policies have had the impact of increasing inequality, certainly in the Public Service. Therefore 1 cannot justify this legislation on the grounds that the Government is borrowing money that will fulfil worth-while human purposes and result in greater equality between men and women in the work place.
If I thought that this legislation concerned rational economic policies for the country, I might be able to approve of it. However, when one considers the budget which was recently passed through the House, the words that stand out are those of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) when he said that he was leaving the lead in economic matters to the private sector. The Government has actually washed its hands of the very tools that could allow it to provide employment for everyone and bring about a real recovery in this country. It has ignored its opportunity to give some energy and thrust to economic activity in the country. I make that point because when one considers a country such as Japan one can see that it learned long ago the lesson of economic planning, which is, that you cannot leave the direction of the over-all economy to the private sector. Unemployment in Japan is currently in the neighbourhood of 3 per cent, while our unemployment rate is well over 12 per cent. We should learn from our neighbours on this planet.
We should understand that we have a responsibility for what happens in our community and our country. We must set objectives and goals and be committee to the importance of employment for every Canadian in order that we might grow as individuals through meaningful work.
If this borrowing authority being requested by Members opposite were put to a useful and sane purpose, 1 would approve of it. So long as the Government washes its hands of economic matters by saying that it no longer takes the responsibility to steer the ship of state and to provide employment for every Canadian, it is incumbent upon Members of this side of the House to condemn the financial activities of the Government. It is important to condemn the amount of money that the Government continually asks for authority to borrow.
The Government's request for this money could be legitimate if it came to the House in good conscience to borrow that money for Canadians so they could meet their own basic human needs and find employment for individuals who are unemployed today. This borrowing request would be acceptable if it were meant to bring about greater equality between men and women, between handicapped and other Canadians
and between natives and the rest of the population. But borrowing without reason is irrational and deserves to be not only questioned but condemned.
I call upon the Government to re-examine its commitment. Rather than attempting to redefine the notion of full employment upwards, which it has been doing lately, it talks participation rates, the regional nature of the country and the difficulty of penetrating foreign markets. All of this talk is an attempt to convince Canadians that it is acceptable to have the number of people unemployed that we have today. That certainly is unacceptable to our Party and unacceptable to a majority of Canadians.
Before the Government comes to the House to ask for borrowing authority it should first examine its purposes and adopt as its first objective the provision of employment for all Canadians and the greater equality for the people in this country.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), lamented the fact that in spite of all the serious problems and challenges facing the nation today and the seeming inability of the Government to react, he felt that the Government did not even realize the seriousness of those problems.
As is my usual custom, on Sunday I went to church. 1 listened to the minister as he referred to the fact that it is sometimes necessary to use dramatic or sensational methods in order to catch the attention of the people before they are willing to listen. He used this illustration: a man had a donkey which was hitched to a cart. No matter what he said to it, it would not move. He kept shouting at it until he got rather disgusted and took a hammer and hit the donkey between the eyes. A bystander asked, "What in the world did you do that for?" Why did you hit the donkey in the head?" He said, "I had to do it to get his attention."
I believe that is similar to the situation we have today. It seems to necessitate the use of some dramatic or sensational effort to get the Government to realize the seriousness of the situation and to act upon it.
I am not implying that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) or anyone else is a donkey. 1 do not know if that would be parliamentary. 1 am not implying that the Minister of Finance is a donkey, but it appears as though he shared that proverbial characteristic of a donkey, that is stubbornness.
It has been pointed out that this is the seventh time that the Government has introduced a measure asking for authority to borrow more money to finance its operations. Therefore, it has been seven times that we have endeavoured to use that hammer of reason to convince the Government that the direction in which it is headed is not the one which will lead us to a satisfactory destination.
Instead, the Government is leading us in the opposite direction. Rather than bringing us out of the problems and difficulties which we face at present, it is driving us deeper into the ground and making the problem even more difficult.
May 26, 1983

The Government has failed to recognize and acknowledge the challenges that have been drawn to its attention and the warnings which have been given to it by successive Auditors General, the Comptroller General, taxpayers of this country and Members of the House. We are convinced that continuing overspending, increasing deficits and massive borrowings could bring this country to economic collapse.
The amounts for which the Government has asked borrowing authority have been placed on the record. They are in the following order: $12 billion, $14 billion, $16 billion, $11 billion, $4 billion, $19 billion and $14.7 billion. Clearly this indicates that this request is not a request to meet an emergency but is consistent with the Government's propensity to overspend. Then, with indecent and unblushing arrogance, it forwards a dunner to the taxpayers of Canada to pay up or face the consequences. Everyone knows that the country has been going through a very difficult period and, although some signs would indicate some slight improvement, I have seen nothing to indicate that anyone is about to celebrate a dawn of a new era. In fact, I saw three economists on the television not long ago. One said that things are looking better, another said just about the opposite, and the third one was in between the other two. He indicated that even among economists, which is perhaps usual, there is such a divergence of opinion that they know nothing more about the situation than any other sectors of the community.
If we reviewed the record of the Government we would find there is little to justify the Government's calling upon the people of Canada to increase the borrowing and the money available to Government. Not only should we consider the following facts: That Gross National Product is falling sharply, that capital investment is to fall again, that manufacturing is at only 63 per cent of capacity, that business bankruptcies continue to increase, that we have record unemployment, that corporate profits are down, that manufacturing and shipments are declining together with inflation-that is the record-but we have to take into account the predictions for the future. Woods, Gordon in its April, 1983 "Business Conditions" report expresses concern that inventory shortages could lead to higher prices. In that document we find this paragraph:
In particular, inventories of many raw materials appear to be exceptionally low and cannot be replenished quickly. The business recovery could trigger sudden bottlenecks and sharp price increases, which could, in turn, touch off renewed fear of inflation, tighter monetary restraint, and rising interest rates.
The record is pitiful, the forecasts are discouraging, yet the Government continues on the course, and rather than improving the conditions of this country it is even threatening to make them much, much worse.
Speaking about the deficits, an article appeared in the paper under the heading "Deficit cuts needed as soon as possible." The article is written by Mr. Ronald Anderson. He pointed out a very significant factor. He wrote:
-the proposed increase in federal spending this year and next, together with the absence of any new spending restraints in later years, will result in an increase in the federal Government's share of the Gross National Product. In 1980, before
Borrowing Authority
the recession, Ottawa absorbed 21 per cent of GNP; in the November, 1981. budget, the federal share was projected to increase to 22 per cent; this proportion now is expected to increase, in the 1983-1984 fiscal year, to 26 per cent.
I want to put more on the record from this article but there are time constraints. However, the C. D. Howe Institute said:
-the federal public debt will rise to 46 per cent of GNP in 1987, compared with 29 per cent in 1982 and 15 per cent in 1975.
This statement concludes with these words:
-the commitment contained in the budget to reduce the deficit is not a convincing one. If the deficit persists, little room will be left for stimulative measures if they are needed in the years ahead.
The Government is moving in such a direction that it is evident that rather than improving the situation it will eventually make it worse. I call upon the Government, without hitting it on the head with a hammer, I beg the Government to take another look at the course it is following and the course it is leading us into and request that it change direction and do something really worth-while for the great nation of which we are a part.
