Bill C-143 asked authority to borrow $19 billion. In between Bill C-143 and Bill C-151 only eight Bills have been introduced. Let us look at the totality of what has happened in this session which started, of course, in April, 1980, and is now well on into its fourth year. We get this cradle of numbers, I said cradle, 1 should have said litany of Bills-Bills C-30, C-59, C-lll, C-125, C-128, C-143 and C-150. They come along like a series.
Last year the Government came before Parliament four times. I suppose this year it says, "Never again", and yet it has come twice with ever increasing gulps. It may be that this is what the Government is going to do in the future if this administration continues for another year. We have been told, on the good authority of the Minister of Finance, that the projected shortages, the Government requirements, will be something like $93 billion by the time we get to 1985-1986. One can understand that the gobbets will be bigger and bigger each year. It may be that the Government is doing a job on the public, accustoming it to a bigger dose every time.
What will be the result of the Bill? Several of my colleagues have indicated what it will do. At the present time there is a carryover of $2 billion for 1982-83, and there is at least $5 billion now. Bill C-143 provided for a carryover of $2 billion

May 26, 1983
Borrowing Authority
for 1983-84. This particular Bill also provides for an unexpended portion of $2 billion to be carried on into 1984-85. What do they do with all this money? Is it an absolute necessity? The public tells us, "halt". I do not know whether the present administration has stuffed cotton wool or noise preventers in its ears. It simply continues to spend and spend and spend. Unfortunately, the expenditures are of a kind that are temporary. There is no lasting effect. There is no multiplier effect, with the possible exception of the $3,000 grant for the acquisition of new homes. That program has come to a halt. While the Minister of Public Works (Mr. LeBlanc) boasts about the increased rate of new home construction, as soon as that program effectively stops, there will be a most dramatic downturn in the construction of new housing units. Canadians lack sufficient confidence in this administration and in economic recovery to say that they will take chances because their employment is insecure. There are still very serious lay-offs. Some of them are reaching very high levels. As soon as one sees serious cuts in mid-management, those below who still have employment in the firms become very, very conscious of just how precarious their employment tomorrow may be.
We are going through a very unbalanced time. What this massive borrowing will do to the domestic market of savings, I do not know. It could be that this will wipe out a lot of funds sitting in pension plans and others that are not normally active in industrial investment. Certainly I think it is the Government's good fortune that at this time the industrial demand for funds for investment is not as high as it might be, because there is a great deal of unused capacity and uncertainty as to the value of future investment and the Government has more freedom of action in the sale of its bonds. What the Provinces will do under the circumstances is hard to say. In view of the fact that the Government only needed about $10.7 billion in order to arrive at a fair balance of figures, why must there be a cushion of an additional $2 billion?
When we talk about $2 billion, we are not talking about a weekend's expenditures. For the likes of Hon. Members of the House and most of the public, $2 billion is a great deal of money. It is difficult to provide for a $2 billion carryover, but personally I think it is totally wrong for the Government to come at this time and ask for this much money. The Government must become accountable, and to that extent I am opposed to the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I am both pleased to speak on this Bill and not pleased. I represent constituents who are very concerned.

Farmers, business people and other taxpayers are as concerned as Members of Parliament about the additional borrowing of $14 billion.
It is significant to note that when I came to this House four years ago, the total debt of the Government of Canada was $78 billion. Today the total debt is almost $160 billion. The increased debt for each man, women and child is in excess of $800, and for each taxpayer it is in excess of $1,700. These figures are very alarming.
It is not enough to just point out the problem. There must be a solution. We on this side of the House have some very positive solutions regarding the direction in which this country has been going. One of the major vacuums in this place is the complete lack of understanding of supply-side economics. We must stimulate the private sector to create wealth in this country. You cannot continue spending money to create jobs or in any other direction that is not, in return, building and strengthening this country.
We have a very serious problem in Canada. Governments are too loose with the taxpayers' money. I represent an agricultural riding. Productivity is very imporant in my riding. Productivity has been eroded by the reckless spending by Government. We see this in our oilfields and farms. Taxpayers now find there is not a great deal of incentive to work and to produce, basically because taxation is so high. When an employee works overtime, he finds that he is taxed to death by the income tax department. There is no incentive to produce. As a result, the balance of payments in the country has dropped to a level where we cannot compete in many ways in the international marketplace.
1 believe that we must take a whole new look at production, a whole new look at taxation in Canada. The Government's whole taxation program is counterproductive in many areas of society, and particularly in the House.
One area of expenditure that the Government does not seem to be concerned with is the larger bureaucracy which is being created year by year, day by day, in the House of Commons. It is significant to note that while 5 per cent and 6 per cent guidelines were created, many members of our society, and particularly farmers, realize that they face increased costs of production along with dropping world prices for wheat or beef, or whatever it is that they produce, and in that case, the six and five guideline is not there. But the bureaucrats are protected by the 5 per cent and 6 per cent increase, and if one makes a wage of $70,000 and gets a 6 per cent increase, that is a pretty healthy increase, Mr. Speaker. This is happening year after year at the expense of the taxpayer.
Somewhere down the line, there must be some accountability to the taxpayer by the Government, and I as one Member of the House believe that the Government and each Member sitting in the House owes a great deal of responsibility to the taxpayers of the country. We in the House, and I suppose I am speaking for the Government now, have not in many cases

May 26, 1983
Borrowing Authority
been accountable to productive people who have found it difficult to pay the kind of taxes that are demanded of them by the Government of the country. I call upon the Government to be more accountable to the taxpayers and to bring into practice some incentive program for production that will allow this Government to decrease some of the heavy-handed taxes which have been placed upon the people of Canada.
1 suppose that there are many areas which I could look at in terms of expenditure. I have already mentioned a couple of items like the large bureaucracy that the Government carries and the circulation of funds in many areas. In latter years, the Auditor General has spoken out and suggested that Government spending was out of control, that it was not being controlled by the Finance Minister, and yet year after year the deficits have been rising and the budgets have been coming later and greater.
Four years ago when I came to the House of Commons, I believe that the deficit was $13 million. Today we are looking at a $31 billion deficit. Expenditures are out of control, Mr. Speaker. I call on the House to bring them under control. I call on the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), each Cabinet Minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to be accountable to the taxpayers of the country to whom I am sure we owe a debt of responsibility as Members of Parliament.

subtopic: SHIPS AND SHIPPING-PROTEST AGAINST USE OF FOREIGN-OWNED VESSEL ON ATLANTIC COAST
SHIPS AND SHIPPING-PROTEST AGAINST USE OF FOREIGN-OWNED VESSEL ON ATLANTIC COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) apparently did not really understand, or deliberately chose to evade my question about vessels of foreign ownership or registry being permitted into this country. The Canada Shipping Act does give the Minister of Transport authority to do something about foreign vessels of dubious quality and design being allowed to serve as offshore vessels for standby rescue and supply purposes.
I want to read into the record Section 22 of Part I of this important piece of legislation as the basis for what I am about to say. It is as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in this Part, a ship built outside Canada shall not, without the consent of the Minister, be registered in Canada.
The Minister knows that shipbuilding and ship repair is an important industry in this country. He must know as well, that the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association has been making very sensible recommendations to see that our Canadian interest may be protected. Henry Walsh has been very assiduous in bringing certain things to the attention of the Government.
On September 2, 1980, the Association made a number of proposals for non-subsidy measures of support for the shipbuilding industry. Proposals No. 9 and No. 10 recommend the banning of importation of old vessels, and No. 9 reads as follows:
Fishing vessels over five years of age should be prohibited from importation into Canada.
Proposal No. 10 says:
"All other vessels over ten years of age should be prohibited from importation into Canada."
Even so, we have the current example of an old, obsolete Norwegian whaling ship being brought in to Halifax by the Karlsen Shipping Company Ltd. and undergoing sea trials in Halifax harbour. At the same time, as I pointed out to the Minister yesterday, Ferguson Industries Ltd. of Pictou, Nova Scotia, has been attempting to secure a charter for a vessel that it has extensively modified in order to make it suitable to fit in with offshore oil and gas development and the attendant regulation. You would think that the Government and the Minister would be anxious to help an industry like this in an area of Canada that suffers from high unemployment. Apparently that is not the case.
On January 6, 1983, the Government of Canada announced a series of measures to promote Canadian shipbuilding, including the extension of custom and excise laws for goods used in resource exploration and development, from the present 12-mile limit out to the limits of Canada's Continental Shelf; the closing of loopholes to existing customs jurisdiction, resulting in a 25 per cent duty to all ships and 20 per cent for offshore drilling rigs, and the retention of the 3 per cent performance improvement grant and the extension of the 9 per cent shipbuilding industry assistance program subsidy for ships delivered by June 30, 1985.
Adjournment Debate
I want to give the Government credit for taking some constructive steps. These measures made some sense, but why is the Minister so slow in acting on other measures that are needed to protect our coastal shipping and our small shipbuilding yards? Frankly, although I like the Minister of Transport,
I am sick and tired of his cordial but very often evasive and ill-informed answers on vital matters. I am also very disturbed at the obvious prejudice being exhibited against small industries in certain parts of my Province of Nova Scotia.
Recently I pointed out that one of the largest employers in Nova Scotia, Hawker Siddeley, Canada, Ltd. situated in Trenton, is not being given fair treatment. Now we have another example of a key industry, again in my constituency, Ferguson Industries Ltd., being prejudiced by the inconsistency, or perhaps even outright negligence of the Department of Transport in not putting Canadian marine interests first.
The sensible thing to do is to take some of the actions that other countries have taken to inhibit fishing vessels of over five years of age, and other obsolete vessels over ten years of age from coming into service in our waters. If nothing is done these kinds of vessels can come in under international rules and conventions in the absence of any specific ban or controls by Canada.
Our fleet is aging so we need modern and upgraded vessels. Our shipyards can do the job. As usual, it is the indifference of the Department of Transport and the carelessness of the Minister that is making it hard for them to get on with this type of program. Once more I ask the Minister and his officials to read the very sensible proposals made by the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association, and, after reading them, to do something positive.
The Department of Immigration, I might add, should also take a very close look at some of the practices being followed in allowing mariners from other countries to come in and take jobs from Canadian seamen. Certain companies often advertise very complex job descriptions which are not really indicative of the actual work which has to be done, and use that as a basis for taking in mariners from other countries, often the United Kingdom, to do jobs that could be done just as well and sometimes better by Canadian seamen.
I hope the Government will do something about this because it is ironic that, at a time when we are discussing the borrowing of billions of dollars, a little bit of help to some of the indigenous industries we have could generate some wealth in this country and stop the financial hemorrhaging which sees Parliament tied up in a constant parade of Borrowing Authority Bills.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: SHIPS AND SHIPPING-PROTEST AGAINST USE OF FOREIGN-OWNED VESSEL ON ATLANTIC COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will take the Hon. Member's representation for review by my Minister and also by officials of the Department.

May 26, 1983
Adjournment Debate
The Government's policy, as the Hon. Member knows, is to support an environment whereby shippers and shipowners have freedom to make commercial choices with a minimum of interference from Government. Surely that policy should be supported by the Hon. Member. This allows shipowners, for example, to purchase vessels from the cheapest source. This policy is consistent with Canada's international position on free trade. However, this policy of minimal interference does not prevent the Canadian Government from taking steps to protect shipping interests in Canada.
On January 6, 1983, the Government announced policies to extend and modify the coasting trade regime, thereby providing greater opportunities for Canadian flag vessels to work, increasing employment opportunities for Canadians. At the same time an extension of the customs and excise regime to the offshore was announced which will encourage the building of more ships in Canada. I was pleased that the Hon. Member gave the Government credit for that. This will support the new shipbuilding policy which extends the shipbuilding assistance program until July 1, 1985, and which provides for duty rates on ships operating in Canadian coasting activities of 20 per cent to 25 per cent of the fair market value.
With particular reference to the Rescue Kim, standard procedures must be followed by those wishing to register ships in Canada. Entry is not normally denied to ships which meet the ownership criteria and Canadian safety standards, which are among the highest in the world. The Rescue Kim has followed normal procedures and has complied with coastguard requirements.
The Government is concerned about Canadian shipping interests and, until new legislation is introduced into the House, all applications for foreign ships to work in Canadian waters, either temporarily or permanently, are being monitored closely. However, it is not the intention, through powers given by the Minister under the Canada Shipping Act or otherwise, to embark on a program of import restrictions that could be contrary to Canada's international obligations under GATT.

subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN TRANSPORTATION ACT-REPORT OF PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENTS. (B) POSITION OF PRIME MINISTER
WESTERN GRAIN TRANSPORTATION ACT-REPORT OF PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENTS. (B) POSITION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am thankful for this opportunity to respond to an answer I received from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during Question Period on May 20. This flows from my feelings as a sitting Member in this House representing every man, woman and child in my riding, whether they be Conservative, Liberal, NDP, Communist or Rhinoceros. That is the fundamental tenet underlining the parliamentary system.
When an election is called and the writ is handed down, everyone lines up behind their favourite candidate and goes hell bent for election to get every possible vote so that candidate can arrive here in this House. But once those candidates arrive they become Hon. Members of certain ridings, as I am the Hon. Member for Athabasca. It really upsets me when the
Prime Minister of my country, holding the highest office in this land, goes from one end of the country to the other stating certain things to western producers who question the Crow rate changes because they are going to have such detrimental effects on western farmers.
Mr. Mills represents the cattle producers in Alberta. The Edmonton Journal of May 17 states:
Mills said Trudeau told the prairie wheat pools and farmer and cattle industry representatives "he didn't think this was the best solution they could come up with . . . not the best economic solution".
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was admitting that the Crow was bad.
I would also like to quote from the Edmonton Journal of May 19, which states:
At his recent Jasper dinner to discuss freight rates, Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau told agriculture industry representatives legislation to replace the Crow will not be changed to suit the West because the region "can't deliver Liberal votes in Parliament".
It is easy to be outraged at a statement from the Prime Minister of my country to western producers because they happen to vote NDP or Conservative. I see two Hon. Members sitting across the way who think that this is a big joke.

subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN TRANSPORTATION ACT-REPORT OF PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENTS. (B) POSITION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Come with me to my riding and speak to some of the producers who are going bankrupt. They are upset because of the Crow debate and the change in statutory freight rates which will actually increase their shipping costs by 500 per cent within three years. Just think of that, 500 per cent! Yet people have come from across Canada to march on the House of Commons because they had mortgage rates which, when they renewed them, rose by 100 per cent. In some cases, their mortgage payments doubled. They marched on this House, they made their feelings known, and legislation was brought in to help these people. They were helped by the Provinces and by this Government.
In the last two years input costs to the farmer, the producer in western Canada, indeed in all of Canada, have increased four fold or five fold. They are hit with high energy costs.
One might think that increase applies only to gasoline and diesel fuel. Of course, it does not. One of the largest single outlays of a producer is the cost of the fertilizer he uses when he plants in the spring. Where does the fertilizer come from? It comes from plants that are users of energy. The energy is being taxed. Fertilizer comes from Petrosar and some of those plants which are paying the wellhead tax, the petroleum gas revenue tax. All of those taxes are included in the price of the very basic commodity of the fertilizer.
The producer must use diesel fuel to move his machinery around. Where does that fuel come from? He pays the same amount for his diesel fuel as the trucker or anyone who drives a diesel car. There are increased gasoline taxes. The Government is hitting the farmer with all those taxes, not recognizing
May 26, 1983

or considering the fact that the farmer produces from renewable resources-constantly renewing-and adds to the balance of payments of this country by something like $8 billion.
Yet the Prime Minister goes out to western Canada and says, "1 know that this is not the solution", and he shrugs. "I know that this is not the best economic solution for the producers in western Canada, but they cannot produce votes in western Canada. You people cannot produce Liberal votes". That underlines a feeling in this House.
1 had a totally different perception when I came to Ottawa. I felt that 1 would be able to work hand in hand with many of my colleagues on the other side and, indeed, many of my colleagues in the NDP. At times, we have sat on committees and have done that. It must be at the direction of the Prime Minister and a bankrupt front bench that the Government has taken this different attitude toward these matters that have come before the House for discussion.
SIS)
The Government has now introduced a borrowing authority Bill through which something like $4 billion or $5 billion will be held in reserve to be used to buy votes. 1 was aware that this does happen, but I was surprised to see it done so blatantly.
It is totally bankrupt, immoral and unjustified on the part of the Prime Minister to go to western Canada and say such a thing to producers who are worrying about their very livelihood, about losing their farms, who fear they will not be able to pass their family farms on to their children because they foresee bankruptcy as a result of a change in statutory freight rates that the Government is forcing through under closure. He has the unmitigated gall to tell those people, "You cannot deliver votes, therefore the Bill will go through."
Mir. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport): Mr. Speaker, I could not agree more with the Hon. Member when he says that once a Member arrives in the House he or she represents every Canadian in that riding. If we expand that, the Prime Minister and this Parliament represent all Canadians across Canada.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did not say what the Hon. Member suggests. If the Hon. Member spent more time in the House, and it has been quite some time since I have seen him in his seat, although I am pleased to see him here during the Adjournment Debate, he would not misquote the Prime Minister as he has today in an attempt to score a few political points. I think it is a disgrace that the Hon. Member stands in his place and misquotes the Prime Minister of Canada the way he has done tonight.
I think the Crow rate debate involves a very emotional issue. I think we can categorize it into two areas. The first is whether there should be a change. I think most organizations across Canada agree that there has to be change. Even those organizations which want no change, proceed to give five or six points they would like to see changed in the Bill. They are saying, "yes, give us the Bill but with these changes." I suggest that we have come a long way in an effort to accommodate those amendments that Canadians, especially those out west,
Adjournment Debate
have asked for. Whether there should be change is not negotiable. There must be change.
The second element of the Crowsnest debate is what sort of change should take place. The bigger question is what change is considered desirable. It is clear that on this question there are deeply held differences of views in the west and across Canada.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) have been candid in admitting that the original proposal was perhaps better-that is what the Prime Minister was saying out west-but that the present proposal under Bill C-155 is still considerably better than doing nothing, which is what the Hon. Member and the NDP want to do. His Party does not want to do that. Their official critic and Members speaking on that side have been saying we should bring the Bill to committee, but with changes. I do not know where the Member has been during these weeks, because he seems to be missing what his own Party is asking for. His Party is not rejecting the Bill outright. It is saying to bring in the Bill but with some changes.
I urge the Opposition to understand the need for the revision of the Crow rate to allow for the upgrading of the western rail transportation system. It is important to all Canadians that this legislation should pass.

subtopic: INCOME TAX-DEDUCTIONS FOR CHILD CARE EXPENSES. (B) REQUEST THAT TAX CREDIT REPLACE CURRENT PROVISION
INCOME TAX-DEDUCTIONS FOR CHILD CARE EXPENSES. (B) REQUEST THAT TAX CREDIT REPLACE CURRENT PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to elaborate on my question of May 2 to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde).
The child care expense deduction is intended to help defray expenses incurred for the care of children under 14 while parent or parents are working. The system of providing some relief for child care costs through the current tax deduction is inadequate, inequitable and discriminatory. The Minister's answers were also inadequate.
A change to the child care expense deduction proposed in the April budget which removes one discriminatory aspect of this deduction creates a new and more insidious discrimination against the unemployed. Prior to the April budget any working mother could claim the deduction, regardless of the husband's presence or absence, and regardless of his activities, whether he was working, studying or unemployed. However, a man could claim the deduction only if his wife was clearly not available to care for the children, one circumstance being separation. In addition, the man had to meet stricter requirements, such as legal proof of separation. No one would deny that it is overwhelmingly women who assume child care responsibilities, or that the law was seen to reinforce the traditional view that women are responsible for child care, but as well created inequities for some fathers.
The budget proposes to remove sex discrimination from the Income Tax Act and make the child care expense deduction

May 26, 1983
Adjournment Debate
available equally to men and women. Once the proposed change comes into effect the spouse with the lower income will be required to claim the deduction. For a couple, both spouses must have jobs to be eligible for the deduction, unless one spouse is infirm, in an institution or a full-time student. Before the change a mother could claim the deduction if her husband was laid off or unemployed. When the law is changed neither the mother nor the father will be able to claim it if one of them is unemployed. This is the point I was trying to stress to the Minister.
With a record number of unemployed, this inequity will hurt many Canadian families who require assistance with their child care costs. Many, as I pointed out, have been unemployed for a period of over one year. The lack of child care is often a barrier for women looking for jobs. The costs of child care are even more prohibitive for people without an adequate income or for a family with both parents normally working suddenly faced with only one pay cheque.
The new budget change will be of greater aid to rich mothers. Tax deductions always benefit higher income families more than lower income families. Even though many people in lower income brackets claim this deduction, those in the higher brackets receive a bigger benefit.
An example of how this inequity comes about was mentioned in an article by George Brett in his column "Dollars and Sense" in The Toronto Star on May 2. It referred to two Ontario women, a secretary and a lawyer, each of whom has two children in day care. The low paid secretary when she makes out her 1983 tax return will get back $1,124 while the high paid lawyer will get back $1,776. Doubling the deductions simply increases this inequity and the regressivity of the tradition. Neither women receives anything close to the actual amount she spends on child care costs estimated at $12 a day or $3,200 a year.
There are other problems with the child care expense deduction besides its inherent regressivity. Many people cannot claim the deduction because of the requirement for receipts and the social insurance numbers of the care givers. A large group of parents not claiming the deduction are low income parents who are unable to get the required receipts. While receipts are readily available from day care centres and live in nannies, these types of care are the most expensive and, therefore, used by higher income parents. Lower and middle income families tend to use unlicensed less expensive babysitters who do not provide receipts. More families in the coming year will find that they cannot claim the child care expense deduction if one of them is unemployed.
We believe the Government could have chosen other mechanisms to spend money more equitably on child care. In the 1980 taxation year the cost to the federal Government in forgone revenue was approximately $54 million. This money should be spent in the most equitable manner possible.
The NDP believes that all families regardless of income must have access to affordable quality child care. Our longterm goal is a universally accessible fully funded child care system. In the interim, a refundable child care expense tax
credit would be the most equitable system. This conclusion was supported by the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in 1970, by the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, the National Action Committee and many other groups across the country. The National Council of Welfare and the Canadian Council on Social Development have long been calling for a restructuring of the child benefit system. The Government should stop ignoring good advice and act to create a better system of contributing to child care costs.
1 am sure, Mr. Speaker, being very interested in child care services yourself, you will agree with this.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: INCOME TAX-DEDUCTIONS FOR CHILD CARE EXPENSES. (B) REQUEST THAT TAX CREDIT REPLACE CURRENT PROVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has raised four points which I would like to address very quickly. First of all she claimed that the new measure discriminates against unemployed people. For the second time I would like to clarify for her that this is not the case. The work status of the taxpayer is irrelevant. The income level of the taxpayer is the only relevant standard applied here. The taxpayer cannot claim more than two-thirds of earned income under this deduction. If a taxpayer with two children wants the full $4,000 deduction, that taxpayer must have $6,000 of declared earned income; from where it comes is irrelevant. Whether it is unemployment insurance, private income or working income is irrelevant. It must simply be no more than two-thirds of earned income. That is the only test.
Second, she said that in the past we discriminated against fathers. That was true, and that discrimination was removed in the budget.
Third, she said that the budget measures discriminate between rich and poor. I ask her to look at the other measures which are connected very directly in the budget to this one. For example the employment expense credit can only be used to its fullest impact by low income earners, by people who earn up to $16,000. People with incomes beyond that level do not obtain the full benefit of that deduction. The high Child Tax Credit is being continued and indexed fully because of our concern for lower income workers.
Finally she said that low income people cannot obtain receipts for their child care expenses. She should recognize in those circumstances that the people providing the child care will not give receipts because they do not want to pay income tax. She is asking us to approve and to continue a system of cheating. We are not about to do that.
I would like to close with the observation that I agree with her that there should be a full system of child care available from the day of infancy until a child graduates from school. I ask her to join with the Government and with other spokesmen to pressure some of the provincial Governments into accepting their responsibility. We pay half the cost of the Canada Assistance Program and the other cost sharing efforts in this regard, and it is about time people like the Honourable Bill Davis in Ontario accepted their full responsibilities under these measures.
